title: Water from snow and ice
summary: Melting snow and ice gives drinking water when taps and wells stop, but it is slow and takes about twice the heat of boiling liquid water, and more in cold and wind. Use ice or old packed snow, start with water in the pot, and treat the meltwater: snow is not clean, and roadside snow carries chemicals boiling can't remove. Don't eat snow: it costs body heat.

materials.item: Pot with a lid, as wide as the stove safely takes
Liquid water to start the pot
materials.qty: about 2.5 cm (1 in) deep in the pot

materials.item: Shovel, scoop, and a bucket or clean bag kept for snow only
Clean containers with caps for the meltwater
Fuel for a stove or fire, or a wood stove already burning
Plain unscented household bleach, for when you can't boil
Clean cloth or coffee filter to strain grit

steps.text: Look for open water or a safe hole in lake ice first; melting snow is the slow, fuel-hungry choice (TC 21-3, MSR alpine).
Gather ice, or old packed snow from deep in a drift, white and clean, upwind of toilets and garbage, and away from where pets go (TC 21-3, MSR alpine, Wyoming SWE).
steps.warn: Never use snow from roadsides, plough banks or parking lots: it can hold road salt, oil and heavy metals (TAC snow), and boiling or bleach won't make water with toxic chemicals safe (CDC emergency).

steps.text: Melt where the fumes go outside: on a wood stove top indoors, or on a camp stove outdoors. See [Cooking indoors in a winter outage](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors).
steps.warn: Camp stoves, barbecues and charcoal make carbon monoxide, which can kill in an enclosed space. Keep them out of tents, snow shelters, vehicles and garages, even for one pot (MSR PR Deluxe, TC 21-3).

steps.text: Pour about 2.5 cm (1 in) of water into the pot before any snow goes in, and before you light the stove (MSR alpine).
steps.warn: On a canister-top gas stove like MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe, never run a dry pot and never put a windscreen round it: the canister can overheat and explode (MSR PR Deluxe).

steps.text: Add snow a handful at a time, press it down into the water, and keep the lid on between handfuls (TC 21-3, MSR fuel).
Pour off meltwater as the pot fills, leaving some in the bottom for the next batch, until you have enough.
If the water is cloudy or gritty, let it settle and pour off the clear part, or strain it through a clean cloth.
Bring it to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute, or 2 minutes above 2,000 m (HealthLinkBC 49b).
steps.warn: Lift a full pot of boiling water with dry mitts and set it down on something steady: a tipped pot scalds.

steps.text: If you can't boil it, add plain unscented bleach: 2 drops per litre of 5–9 % bleach, doubled to 4 for water under 10 °C, and wait 1 to 2 hours. It should smell faintly of chlorine afterwards; if not, add 2 more drops per litre and wait 15 minutes more (CDC emergency, HealthLinkBC 49b).
Store it in clean, capped containers in the warm room, part-full in case they freeze, and make tomorrow's water before bed (TC 21-3).
Drink it, warm if you can, and keep drinking through the day; don't eat snow or ice (TC 21-3).

notes:
## Ice first, fresh snow last
Snow is mostly air. Wyoming's snow survey office puts new snow at about 8–10 % water; once it has lain on the ground and settled, about 30 % (Wyoming SWE). Ice is about 90 % as dense as water (USGS density). The US Army's cold-weather handbook puts it plainly: ice gives more water in less time than snow (TC 21-3).

| What fills a 10 L pot | Water out, roughly | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Fresh, fluffy snow | about 1 L | 8–10 % water (Wyoming SWE) |
| Old, settled snow | about 3 L | settled snow is about 30 % water (Wyoming SWE) |
| Chunks of clear ice | most of the pot, less the gaps between chunks | about 90 % as dense as water (USGS density) |

Look for the dense stuff: the lower layers of an old drift or bank, crusted snow, and ice chipped from a clean pond or lake, but only where the ice is safe to stand on. Better still, skip melting: TC 21-3 and MSR both say to take water from open streams or lakes where you can, to save time and fuel (TC 21-3, MSR alpine). See [Getting water through lake and river ice](#guides/skill_water_through_ice).

## Where to gather it
- **Clean, white snow only.** TC 21-3 sets aside a snow area upwind of camp and away from latrines and garbage, and says never to use discoloured snow (TC 21-3). MSR's writer digs about 30 cm (1 ft) below the surface for fresh snow and steers clear of dirty or discoloured patches (MSR alpine).
- **Not from roadsides, plough banks or parking lots.** Snow cleared from roads carries road salt and other de-icers, oil, grease and heavy metals from vehicles, litter, dirt and airborne pollutants (TAC snow). Boiling and bleach can't make water with fuel or toxic chemicals safe (CDC emergency); TAC adds that there is currently no practical or economical way to remove the chlorides found in snow (TAC snow).
- **Roof snow** can carry what roof rain does: CDC lists dirt and germs, bird droppings, and chemicals such as lead or copper from roofing, gutters and pipes (CDC rainwater). Treat it like roof rainwater, and don't use snow from a roof you wouldn't collect rain from: see [Rainwater collection from a roof](#guides/build_rainwater_collection).
- Keep a scoop and a bucket or bag for snow only, and gather away from the toilet area, the woodpile and where pets go.

## Melting without scorching
Snow alone in a hot pot scorches the bottom. MSR's writer adds snow only to a pot that already has some water in it for that reason, and warns that a pot poured or pumped completely dry can scorch too (MSR alpine). So start with about 2.5 cm (1 in) of water in the pot, then add snow a little at a time and keep adding as it melts. Water first is MSR's advice; TC 21-3 starts with a small amount of snow in the pot and adds more as it melts (MSR alpine, TC 21-3). Press the snow down into the water and keep the lid on: MSR's own fuel advice is to use a lid and not keep lifting it (MSR fuel). When you pour off, leave some water in the pot for the next batch.

On a canister-top stove, where the burner screws straight onto the gas can, an empty pot is a danger, not only a burnt pot. MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe instructions say never to run the stove with empty or dry cookware and never to put any kind of windscreen round it, because either can make the canister explode (MSR PR Deluxe). Put the water in before you light it.

## What it costs in fuel
Melting is the expensive part. Melting 1 kg of ice takes 334 kJ, as much as warming that water from 0 °C to about 80 °C (OpenStax). Taking snow at −10 °C up to a boil needs about 0.77 MJ per litre, against about 0.38 MJ to boil a litre of water from 10 °C: roughly double, worked from OpenStax's figures. Outdoors it gets worse: MSR plans on 3–4 times its normal fuel for low temperatures, wind and melting snow (MSR fuel). TC 21-3 says melting and boiling enough snow for a drink can take 30 to 40 minutes, so run every stove you have and make the next morning's water before bed (TC 21-3).

To spend less:
- Melt on a wood stove that is already burning to heat the house: see [Cooking on a wood stove](#guides/skill_cook_on_wood_stove).
- Use a wide pot with a lid, out of the wind.
- On a sunny day, a container of snow wrapped in dark cloth and left in the sun melts slowly with no fuel at all (Utah Health).
- Per-fuel numbers for wood, gas, alcohol, kerosene and electricity are in [What boiling water costs in fuel](#guides/reference_cooking_fuel).

Camp stoves, barbecues and charcoal stay outdoors, even for a quick pot of snow: see [Cooking indoors in a winter outage](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors).

## Treat it: snow is not clean
Freezing does not kill or remove germs (HealthLinkBC 49b), so snow and ice keep whatever fell or blew onto them. Treat meltwater like any surface water:
1. **Clear it.** If it's cloudy or gritty, let it settle and pour off the clear part, or strain it through a cloth.
2. **Boil it:** a rolling boil for at least 1 minute; above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), at least 2 minutes (HealthLinkBC 49b). The 1986 army handbook says 15 minutes (TC 21-3); current health advice is 1 minute, which saves a lot of fuel.
3. **Or chlorinate it** with plain household bleach: not scented, colour-safe, with added cleaners, or non-chlorine bleach (HealthLinkBC 49b). For 5–9 % bleach, 2 drops per litre; for 1 % bleach, 10 drops (CDC emergency). Meltwater is colder than 10 °C, so double the dose and let it stand 1 to 2 hours (HealthLinkBC 49b). Chlorine does not reliably kill Cryptosporidium (CDC Yellow Book), so boil when you can. Old bleach is weak: [Test bleach strength](#guides/test_bleach_strength). After the wait the water should smell faintly of chlorine; if it doesn't, add 2 more drops per litre and wait another 15 minutes (HealthLinkBC 49b). Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or other cleaners: it gives off toxic gas (Health Canada chemicals). See [Chemicals reference](#guides/reference_chemicals).
4. **A germ filter** must not have frozen, and most don't stop viruses: see [Keeping water liquid in winter](#guides/skill_water_in_winter) and [Water filters: what they remove](#guides/reference_water_filters).

## Don't eat snow
TC 21-3 tells soldiers not to eat snow or ice because it lowers the body's core temperature (TC 21-3). A University of Utah emergency doctor adds that snow holds so little water that it takes about 8 to 10 quarts of it to give a quart of water, and that the body spends its own energy melting it (Utah Health). In numbers: melting enough snow to make 1 L of water (about 8 to 10 L of fresh snow, by Utah Health's figure) and warming it from 0 °C to body temperature (37 °C) takes about 490 kJ (about 117 kcal) of body heat, worked from OpenStax's figures, and more when the snow is colder. For someone cold and short of food, that is heat they can't spare: see the [cold card](#browse/hazards/cold). Melt it first, and warm it if you can. Children grab snow without thinking; give them a warm drink instead.

## How much to make
People lose a lot of fluid in the cold, and drinking only when thirsty doesn't keep up (TC 21-3). The handbook asks for at least 3.5 US quarts (about 3.3 L) a day during heavy work, as much of it hot as possible (TC 21-3). For a household, Get Prepared plans on about 4 L per person per day for drinking, cooking and sanitation (Get Prepared kits). Keep what you've melted from freezing again: see [Keeping water liquid in winter](#guides/skill_water_in_winter).
